fields.features_heading: Inside the Relationship Quiz Emergent Builds
fields.features_subheading: Describe the quiz in one prompt, and Emergent builds the questions, the results, and the table that stores every answer.
fields.feature_1:
Partners answer about each other

Each partner answers every question twice: once for themselves, once guessing the other. The app counts every guess that lands on the partner's own answer and scores it out of 12.
fields.feature_2:
A connection style as the result

Switch to a matching quiz, where every option points to a style such as Easy Routines. The result screen names the style the answers lean toward and explains it in two lines.
fields.feature_3:
Answers saved without names

Leave the name field out for a workshop, and the app stores each set of answers on its own. The facilitator sees how many people landed on each result, never who chose what.
fields.feature_4:
Each finished quiz is a row

Every completed quiz lands in a database you own, with each pick and the result next to it. Sort by result before a session, or filter for the couples who scored under 8.
fields.feature_5:
Built for a phone on the couch

Couples tap through one question per screen with a progress bar, which suits a link opened on two phones side by side. Emergent sets no cap on how many people take the quiz.
fields.feature_6:
An alert when someone finishes

Ask for an email or Slack message each time a visitor finishes the quiz, with their result in the first line. Publish on a custom domain, included with Emergent and using credits.

fields.usecase_heading: Four Ways to Run a Relationship Quiz
fields.tab_content_1:
Who knows whom best: the Brandts, 11 of 12

Priya Okonjo and Tomas Novak invited 4 couples to game night and sent out one link. Each partner answered 12 questions about the other, and a guess that matched the partner's own answer scored 1 point. The final board put Leah and Sam Brandt first at 11 of 12 and June and Ravi Chandran last at 6 of 12.

Riverside Community Center sends the quiz to 18 couples in its premarriage workshop. No names are stored, so facilitator Dana Mercer sees the tally: Conversation First 14, Shared Projects 9, Easy Routines 8, New Experiences 5. Talk leads at 14 of 36 partners, and week 1 opens with hard conversations.
fields.tab_content_3:
An intro call request lands with the result attached

Elena Carvalho found coach Andre Whitfield's site and took the relationship quiz on it. Her answers leaned toward Easy Routines, and the result screen offered a 20-minute intro call. She booked one, and the email alert to Andre carried her name and her result.
fields.tab_content_4:
20 pairs made by result at the door

Kim Laurent hosts a monthly singles mixer and asks all 40 guests to take the relationship quiz as they check in. The app groups guests who landed on the same connection style and posts 20 pairs for round 1. Nobody has to open with the weather.

fields.howto_title: How to Build a Relationship Quiz
fields.howto_description: Seven steps to build a relationship quiz that fits its room, from picking the format to checking where every answer lands.
fields.howto_step_2_title: 02 Pick a match score or a style result
fields.howto_step_1_des: Choose what the quiz is for before you write a question: a party game, a workshop conversation, or an intake for coaching. That one choice decides what the result screen says and what you keep afterward.
fields.howto_step_2_des: Pick scored matches when two partners answer about each other and the ending is one number out of 12. Pick a style result when anyone can answer alone and the ending names how they connect. Emergent builds either from one sentence in the prompt.
fields.howto_step_3_des: Ask about moments both partners have lived: a free Tuesday evening, the last disagreement, who plans the trips. Specific moments get honest picks, and they turn into options people recognize on the first read instead of labels they have to decode.
fields.howto_step_4_des: Give every option a job. In a scored quiz, each question holds the partner's own answer and the guess about it. In a style quiz, point each option at exactly one result. Then no answer set can end in a tie you did not plan.
fields.howto_step_5_des: Decide whether a name is stored with each set of answers. A game night wants names on the board, and a workshop wants none. Say so in the prompt, and the table keeps exactly the fields you asked for and nothing else.
fields.howto_step_6_title: 06 Run it with one couple first
fields.howto_step_6_des: Run the quiz with one couple before the room fills. Two people finish in under 5 minutes and surface the question that reads two ways, the option nobody picks, and the result text that lands wrong. Fix each one by prompting, then lock the link.
fields.howto_step_7_title: 07 Share one link and watch the table
fields.howto_step_7_des: Share one link by text or a QR code at the door. Each finished quiz arrives as a row while the room is still playing, and you can call the winners, post the pairs, or plan the first session the same night.

faq_plan.a: A relationship quiz is a short set of questions a couple or one person answers about how a relationship runs day to day. It ends in a score, when partners guess each other's answers, or in a named style, when every option points at one result.

faq_plan.q: How do I create a relationship quiz?
faq_plan.a: Describe it in one sentence to Emergent's AI survey builder: who answers, what the questions cover, and what the result screen says. Emergent builds the quiz, the result screens, and a table that holds every response, and a follow-up prompt changes any question or result.

faq_plan.q: What does a relationship compatibility quiz measure?
faq_plan.a: It measures how far two partners' answers line up on the same questions: habits, plans, free time, and how each one recharges. Agreement counts toward a shared score, and the gaps make better conversation starters than the matches. No quiz settles whether two people fit; it shows where to look first.

faq_plan.q: Can I run a healthy relationship quiz without scoring people?
faq_plan.a: Yes. Write a healthy relationship quiz whose result names a pattern to talk about, not a grade, and let takers skip any question. Keep every option about behavior, not character. For a group that just met, an icebreaker such as a spirit animal quiz warms the room before heavier questions.

faq_plan.q: What questions belong in an am I ready for a relationship quiz?
faq_plan.ref: am i ready for relationship quiz
faq_plan.secondary: am i ready for relationship quiz
faq_plan.a: Ask about the taker's own weeks, not an imagined partner: how free evenings get spent, what happens after an argument, what they would change about last month. Phrase results as what the answers lean toward, never as a verdict on whether someone is ready.

faq_plan.q: Should a relationship quiz for couples show both partners' answers?
faq_plan.a: Show both sets only after both partners have finished, or the second one answers to match. Reveal the matched pairs question by question, and leave the misses for the couple to read together. There are no response caps on Emergent, and a full room can play at once.

faq_plan.q: How do I turn a couples quiz into a relationship game for a party?
faq_plan.a: Add a score and a board. Partners answer about each other, matched guesses earn points, and the board ranks every couple at the end of the night. Cap one round at 12 questions so it fits between dinner and dessert. The same scored format runs a marketing quiz at a trade show booth once the questions change.

faq_plan.q: Can I build an is my relationship toxic quiz without giving advice?
faq_plan.a: Treat that topic with care. loveisrespect, a national advocacy resource, runs a quiz on whether a relationship is healthy, and a worried taker belongs there. A quiz you publish should surface patterns to discuss with someone they trust, never label a partner, and list a real resource on the result screen.

faq_plan.q: Where do relationship quiz answers go after someone hits submit?
faq_plan.a: They land in a table, one row per finished quiz: every pick beside the result and the time. Filter rows before a session, or push each new one to a tool you already use through its API. The table is a database you own on Emergent, and the answers stay yours if you change tools.

faq_plan.q: How many questions should a relationship quiz have?
faq_plan.a: Use 8 to 12. Eight supports a style result, and 12 keeps a scored couples round under 10 minutes. Go shorter for lighter topics: a dog breed quiz can land a result in 6 picks. Cut any question that cannot change the result.

quiz.title: How Your Relationship Connects
quiz.intro: Eight questions about ordinary weeks together. Answer for yourself, and your result names the connection style your answers lean toward, with one thing to plan more of.

questions.text: It is 9 p.m. on a Tuesday and neither of you has plans. What sounds best?

options.text: A long talk that wanders wherever it goes
Finally hanging the shelves together
The usual show from the usual couch spots
A late drive to a diner you have never tried

questions.text: A free Saturday opens up. What do you hope your partner suggests?

options.text: Coffee and a real catch-up, phones away
Repainting the hallway you both keep ignoring
The market loop you always walk
A day trip with the destination kept secret

questions.text: What makes you feel closest after a hard week?

options.text: Talking it through until it makes sense
Fixing or building something side by side
Cooking the meal you always cook
Getting out of town, even for one night

questions.text: Your anniversary is coming up. Which plan would you pick?

options.text: A slow dinner with time to talk
Starting the garden you keep sketching
The restaurant from your first date, same order
Tickets kept sealed until the day arrives

questions.text: You get surprise good news. What is your first move?

options.text: Call your partner and tell the whole story
Start planning what you two could build with it
Save it for dinner, where news always lands
Book something spontaneous to celebrate

questions.text: Which small gift would land best with you?

options.text: A letter that says what usually goes unsaid
A tool for the project you two started
Your regular order, brought home unasked
An envelope with a date and no details

questions.text: What do you want more of in an average month?

options.text: Conversations with no clock on them
Hours spent making something together
Quiet evenings that repeat on purpose
Plans you could not have predicted

questions.text: A disagreement just ended. What helps most now?

options.text: Naming what each of you heard
Doing a small task together to reset
Sliding back into the normal evening rhythm
A walk somewhere neither of you knows

results.title: Conversation First
results.description: Your answers lean toward long talks and thinking out loud together. Closeness shows up in words for you: the catch-up, the debrief, the letter. Plan one evening a week with no clock and nothing scheduled after, and let the conversation wander.

results.title: Shared Projects
results.description: Your answers lean toward making and fixing things side by side. The shelves, the garden, the hallway paint: working toward something together is how time with your partner feels well spent. Keep one unfinished project going, and split the jobs so both of you stay in it.

results.title: Easy Routines
results.description: Your answers lean toward the comfort of a repeated week: the usual show, the usual order, the market loop. Small rituals are how you mark what matters. Protect them on busy weeks, and name them out loud so your partner knows they count.

results.title: New Experiences
results.description: Your answers lean toward firsts: the unplanned drive, the sealed envelope, the town neither of you knows. New ground keeps the two of you curious about each other. Put one unfamiliar plan on the calendar each month, and trade who picks it.
